subsection: 7. The US economy, 1968–1989: Vietnam, the federal deficit, recession and international competition

notes.h: Starting point and key terms: the boom, globalisation and stagflation (Higher Level only)
notes.b: From 1945 to 1968 the United States enjoyed a postwar boom. To follow what went wrong after 1968, you need the basic economic terms and the idea that the US economy was now part of a world market.
points: Until 1968 the US had high growth, low inflation and a dominant place in the world economy, with the dollar at the centre of the Bretton Woods system (the postwar arrangement in which other currencies were tied to the dollar and the dollar was convertible into gold).

Inflation means a general rise in prices. Recession means falling output and rising unemployment. Stagflation is the two troubles together: high inflation with stagnant growth and high unemployment, which is unusual because inflation normally comes with strong demand.

A budget deficit is one year's shortfall when government spending is above revenue. The national debt is all the borrowing built up over the years. A trade deficit means imports are above exports, so it is a different thing from the budget deficit.

Globalisation is the growing integration of national economies through trade, investment and finance. For the US it meant that industries faced Japanese and European rivals, and that the value of the dollar and the price of oil were set in a world market.

Corporate capitalism is an economy dominated by large corporations. Here the position of the big US firms in steel and cars was challenged by foreign competition, and Reagan-era deregulation (removing government controls on prices and entry) changed how some industries operated.
The rust belt is the old industrial region of the Midwest and northeast, whose factories declined. The Sun Belt is the South and West, which grew.
notes.tip: Examiners reward clear definitions that keep similar terms apart. Do not mix up inflation (rising prices), recession (falling output) and stagflation (both together), or the deficit (one year) with the debt (accumulated).

notes.h: Guns and butter: the war and the deficit, 1965 to 1968
notes.b: Johnson tried to pay for a major war (guns) and expanding social programmes (butter) at the same time, without raising taxes. This pushed up demand, prices and federal borrowing and set the pattern for the 1970s.
points: Federal spending on the Vietnam War rose sharply after 1965, and Johnson chose not to raise taxes to pay for it while also expanding the Great Society (his programmes against poverty and for education and health). The war was very costly.
Unemployment was already low, so the economy was near full employment. The extra demand from war and welfare spending could not be met by extra output, and so it pushed up prices.
Because spending rose faster than output, inflation, which had been about 1 per cent in 1964, passed 4 per cent in 1968. Consumer prices began to climb steadily in the late 1960s.
Johnson asked Congress for a tax increase only in 1967. Wilbur Mills, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, made agreement conditional on spending cuts, which delayed the measure.
Congress passed a 10 per cent income tax surtax in June 1968 to restrain spending and reduce the deficit, but it did not stop inflation.
The federal budget deficit grew through the late 1960s and 1970s, so deficits became a persistent feature of US government finance.

The balance of payments (the record of money flowing in and out of the country) also worsened. US military spending abroad and foreign investment sent dollars overseas faster than exports earned them.
Foreign governments, notably France, began to exchange dollars for US gold, so the strain on the dollar built through the late 1960s.
notes.tip: A common essay question asks how war spending led to inflation. Make the link: spending on war and welfare with no tax rise, in an economy already near full employment, meant demand outran supply and prices rose.

notes.h: The end of Bretton Woods, 1971 to 1973
notes.b: By 1971 the strain on the dollar was too great. Nixon ended the link between the dollar and gold, and the system of fixed exchange rates followed it.
points: On 15 August 1971 Nixon suspended the convertibility of the dollar into gold, so foreign governments could no longer swap dollars for gold. This ended the Bretton Woods system.
The same measures imposed a 90-day wage and price freeze and a 10 per cent surcharge on imports.
The US trade balance moved into deficit from 1971, and deficits grew in the 1970s. The country was now buying more from abroad than it sold.
The Smithsonian Agreement of December 1971 tried to fix new exchange rates, but it failed, and currencies were floating (their values set by the market) by 1973.
notes.tip: Date the stages precisely: gold decision and freeze in August 1971, Smithsonian in December 1971, floating by 1973. The dollar link to gold ended in 1971, before the 1973 oil shock, so do not say that the oil crisis ended Bretton Woods.

notes.h: The oil shocks and stagflation, 1973 to 1980
notes.b: Two sudden price rises, in 1973 and 1979, hit an economy already suffering from inflation, and produced stagflation.
points: The Arab members of OPEC (the oil producers' organisation) began an oil embargo on the United States in October 1973 after the Yom Kippur War, and oil prices about quadrupled in 1973 to 1974.
The embargo brought petrol queues at filling stations, and in some states rationing by odd and even number plates. It was lifted in March 1974.
The recession of 1973 to 1975 was the worst since the 1930s, with unemployment about 9 per cent in 1975. Dearer oil raised costs and prices while cutting output, which is how stagflation arose.
Ford's Whip Inflation Now campaign of 1974 relied on voluntary measures and was widely mocked. Carter's first attempts at stimulus did not stop inflation rising again in 1978 and 1979.
The Iranian Revolution of 1978 to 1979 caused a second shock, with oil prices about doubling, which deepened inflation and recession.
Inflation was about 13 per cent in 1980. The combination of high inflation and stagnant growth became known as stagflation.
notes.tip: Exams ask how oil prices led to stagflation. Explain the link, higher energy costs raising prices while cutting output and jobs, and keep the first shock (1973, Yom Kippur War embargo) separate from the second (1979, Iranian Revolution).

notes.h: Energy policy after the oil shocks, 1973 to 1979
notes.b: The oil crises made energy a central economic issue. Governments tried conservation, new institutions and the aim of self-sufficiency, but the US stayed dependent on imports.
points: Nixon's Project Independence (November 1973) aimed to end dependence on foreign oil by 1980, but American oil imports kept rising.
Congress passed a national maximum speed limit of 55 miles per hour in January 1974 to reduce petrol consumption, since slower driving uses less fuel.
The Department of Energy was created in August 1977 under Carter, bringing together federal energy programmes that had been spread across several agencies.
The National Energy Act of 1978 encouraged conservation and phased in higher natural gas prices. It was a compromise reached after long debate in Congress.
Domestic oil production remained below its peak, so the United States depended on imports from the Middle East and other producers for a growing share of its oil by the late 1970s.

notes.h: The rust belt: steel and cars under foreign competition
notes.b: In the 1970s American steel and car makers lost ground to Japanese and European rivals. This is globalisation at work, and the damage fell on the industrial Midwest and northeast, nicknamed the rust belt.
points: The steel industry lost ground to imports from Japan and Europe in the 1970s, and steel mills in the Midwest and northeast reduced production or closed.
Youngstown Sheet and Tube closed its Ohio works in September 1977, costing about 5,000 jobs. It became a symbol of the wider loss of industrial jobs in the region.
Japanese car makers such as Toyota and Honda sold small, fuel-efficient cars. After the oil shocks these were attractive, while Detroit built large cars.
Imports took about a quarter of the American car market by the early 1980s, and Japan overtook the United States as the world's largest car producer in 1980.
Chrysler was saved from bankruptcy in 1979 by federal loan guarantees of 1.5 billion dollars. Lee Iacocca led the company.
The Japanese gains led the Reagan administration to negotiate voluntary export restraints in 1981, in which Japan agreed to limit its car exports to the US.
notes.tip: For a question on competition from Japan and Europe, use one named example (Youngstown, Chrysler, or Toyota and Honda) and explain why it mattered, rather than listing several in passing.

notes.h: Why competitiveness fell, and the regional effects
notes.b: American industry was hit by several causes at once, and the effects were uneven across the country. Some regions lost out while others gained.
points: Historians point to several causes of falling competitiveness: older plant (factories and machinery), weaknesses in management and quality, higher wages and costs than rivals, the high dollar in the early 1980s, and wider global change.
A high dollar makes American exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper at home, which is why it hurt manufacturers in particular.
The US trade balance moved into deficit in the 1970s, and the deficit with Japan grew steadily through the 1980s.

The Plaza Accord of September 1985, agreed by the leading industrial countries (the G5: US, Japan, West Germany, France and Britain), aimed to bring the dollar down to restore the competitiveness of American exports.
Rust belt cities such as Detroit, Cleveland and Youngstown lost jobs, population and tax revenue as factory jobs vanished, while the Sun Belt in the South and West gained.
Growth in service and high-technology jobs, in Silicon Valley in California and in defence-related industries, partly offset the losses in manufacturing.
notes.tip: A strong answer on decline gives a judgement on causes, for example weighing global change against policy choices such as the high dollar, rather than only describing closures.

notes.h: Reaganomics: Volcker, tax cuts and the recession
notes.b: Reagan's economic policy, known as Reaganomics, combined tax cuts, less regulation and higher defence spending. First, though, inflation had to be broken, and that brought a severe recession.
points: Paul Volcker became chairman of the Federal Reserve (the US central bank) in August 1979, appointed by Carter, not Reagan. He raised interest rates very sharply to bring down inflation.

These high interest rates helped to cause the recession of 1981 to 1982. Unemployment rose above 10 per cent in late 1982 (peak about 10.8 per cent), the highest since the Depression, before recovery began in 1983.
Reaganomics rested on supply-side theory, associated with the economist Arthur Laffer. It said that lower tax rates would encourage work and investment and so raise growth.
The Economic Recovery Tax Act of August 1981 cut income tax rates by about 25 per cent over three years, reducing the top rate from 70 to 50 per cent.
In 1981 Reagan also cut spending on some social programmes, such as food stamps and aid to families, while defence spending rose.
The Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act (TEFRA) of 1982 raised some taxes to reduce the deficit, which had grown as the tax cuts took effect.
notes.tip: Define Reaganomics, give two or three measures with years, and give a success and a failure. Do not say that the tax cuts caused the 1981 to 1982 recession: it followed Volcker's high interest rates, and the tax cuts came into effect as recovery began.

notes.h: Deregulation, tax reform and the results of the 1980s
notes.b: Deregulation, which means removing government controls over prices and business, had begun before Reagan. The 1980s then brought a long expansion, but also costly failures and continuing weaknesses.
points: Deregulation continued a trend begun under Carter, including the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 and the Staggers Rail Act of 1980, which reduced government control of transport prices.

Deregulation of the savings and loan institutions (thrifts) in the early 1980s was followed by the Savings and Loan crisis. Hundreds failed, and the federal bailout of 1989 cost taxpayers tens of billions of dollars.
The Gramm-Rudman Act of 1985 tried to force deficit reduction by setting deficit targets.
The Tax Reform Act of 1986 cut the top income tax rate to 28 per cent while removing many deductions (amounts that people could subtract from taxable income).
Economic growth returned strongly in the mid-1980s and inflation fell sharply, though unemployment and the deficit remained issues for the rest of the decade.
The expansion from late 1982 to 1990 created about 18 million jobs, mostly in services, but deficits and uneven gains remained.

notes.b: Tax cuts combined with rising defence spending meant that the government spent far more than it raised. The gap was financed by borrowing, much of it from abroad, which left the US in a new and weaker position.
points: Government spending on defence rose sharply under Reagan, and the tax cuts cut revenue, so the federal budget deficit remained large in every year of his presidency.
The national debt nearly tripled during the 1980s, reaching almost 3 trillion dollars, and the government's interest payments became a major item in the budget.
The strong dollar of the early 1980s drew in large amounts of foreign capital, which financed the deficits but hurt exporters because it made their goods dearer abroad.
In 1985 the United States became a net debtor nation, owing more to foreigners than it owned abroad.

The trade deficit reached about 150 billion dollars in 1987. The Plaza Accord of 1985 aimed to lower the dollar. The Louvre Accord of February 1987 aimed to stabilise exchange rates after the dollar's fall.
On 19 October 1987, Black Monday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by about 22 per cent in a single day. The Federal Reserve responded by providing liquidity (ready cash) to the banking system.
notes.tip: Keep the two accords apart. Only the Plaza Accord (1985) aimed to bring the dollar down; the Louvre Accord (1987) aimed to stop it falling further.

notes.b: The steady rise in living standards of the postwar boom slowed after the early 1970s, and the gains of the 1980s were unevenly shared.
points: Real wages (wages adjusted for rising prices) of production workers stagnated from the early 1970s, so household incomes depended increasingly on more family members working.
The gap between high-income and low-income households widened during the 1980s, as the tax cuts of 1981 and 1986 favoured higher earners and wages for less-skilled workers fell in real terms.
The decline of manufacturing reduced the bargaining power of many manual workers, and the share of workers in unions, already falling since the 1950s, fell faster in the 1980s.
Service jobs in retail and catering paid less than the factory jobs they replaced, and the federal minimum wage was not raised from January 1981 to 1990, so its real value fell.
The poverty rate, which had fallen to about 11 per cent in 1973, rose to around 15 per cent in the early 1980s before easing.
Black unemployment was roughly double white unemployment throughout the period, and urban areas that had lost industries suffered most.

notes.b: The decisive judgement is between the recovery of the 1980s and the longer-term weaknesses. A good answer separates two phases: the boom to 1968, and then stagflation, restructuring and an uneven recovery.
points: Success: supporters of Reagan point to the recovery of growth after 1983, low inflation and the expansion of employment in service industries. The long expansion from late 1982 created about 18 million jobs.
Limit: critics point to the rising national debt, the trade deficit and the loss of manufacturing jobs in steel and cars, which made the United States dependent on foreign capital.
Growth was limited between 1968 and 1989 by the cost of Vietnam and the Great Society, the end of Bretton Woods in 1971, the oil shocks of 1973 and 1979, foreign competition, and deficits.
Winners and losers: the 1970s brought stagflation and falling real incomes for many families, while the wealthy gained most from the tax cuts of the 1980s, so the recovery was uneven.
Historians disagree about whether the decline of manufacturing was an inevitable result of global change or of policy choices, such as the high dollar and the lack of industrial policy.

Paul Kennedy, in The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers (1987), argued that the United States was suffering "imperial overstretch". Optimists pointed to US leadership in computers, services and finance.
notes.tip: In a success-or-decline essay, name each cause with a date and set the post-1983 expansion beside debt, trade deficit and uneven gains, rather than listing events. Historians' views, such as Paul Kennedy and the optimists, add weight to the final judgement.

keyTerms.definition: The growing integration of economies through trade and investment, which in the 1970s and 1980s increased competition from Japan and Europe for US industries.
The system in which large corporations dominate the economy, and whose strength was challenged by foreign rivals and deregulation in this period.
The combination of high inflation and stagnant economic growth and rising unemployment that affected the United States in the 1970s.
Reagan's policy of cutting taxes, reducing regulation and raising defence spending, aimed at restoring economic growth and reducing inflation.
The old industrial regions of the Midwest and northeast, centred on steel and car manufacturing, which lost jobs as those industries declined.
The shortfall of federal government spending over revenue, which grew through the Vietnam War, the Reagan tax cuts and defence build-up.
The September 1985 agreement among the leading industrial countries to lower the value of the dollar and restore the competitiveness of US exports.
The postwar monetary order with fixed exchange rates tied to the dollar, which ended in August 1971 when the dollar was no longer convertible to gold.
The theory behind Reaganomics that cutting taxes on income and investment would stimulate production and so raise growth.
The failure of hundreds of thrift institutions in the 1980s after deregulation, which led to a federal bailout in 1989.

factCards.definition: He suspended the convertibility of the dollar into gold and imposed a temporary wage and price freeze.
